paper_title: Trace Hermitian Codes Have Vanishing Bias
statement: A natural approach for getting explicit codes close to the GV bound is to start with such a code over a constant alphabet, and, somehow reduce the alphabet size. Concatenation is a natural candidate, but it seems it is not strong enough to approach the GV bound. Trace codes are also natural candidates, but the results obtained so far are poor. A natural question is whether these results can be improved: Is there a natural subclass of polynomials for which the code described before Theorem 1.1 is close to the GV bound? If we work over the Hermitian function field, and our set of evaluation functions also allows polynomials in x or y alone, then the relative bias of the Trace Hermitian code cannot be better then the relative bias of the Trace RS code. To see that suppose f is a non-square polynomial in Fq [x] of degree d that has bias e over Fq . As every x ∈ Fq has p rational solutions in y that do not affect f , we get a bias of ep over the Hermitian curve, which has the same relative bias. Using Weil bound the bias we know for the Trace RS √ code is O(d q). Lifting this to the Hermitian curve (by taking a polynomial that only depends on one variable) we get an absolute bias of Ω(dq). For some minor restriction on √ the evaluation polynomial we can bound the bias of Trace Hermitian curve by O( dpq), √ which is worse (as d < p). Is it possible to improve the bound we get for the Trace Hermitian curve to O(dq)? Finally, is it possible to improve the bound if we restrict to a subclass of monomials, e.g., monomials with odd degree both in x and y?

We believe the techniques we develop are of independent interest. Our results on Trace AG codes, in the interesting case of high genus curves, greatly improve prior work. We also believe there is much more to learn and understand about the surprising behavior of derivatives in function fields. Our techniques (and the derivative-fix-lemma in particular) allow us to study not only the trace of the Hermitian curve, but also the trace of the codes in the first few levels of the Hermitian tower. We do not state these results because technically they get more involved. Recently, Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Noam Goldgraber and Tomer Manket [7] generalized the techniques in our paper to general AG curves. At a very high level, the techniques of this paper and of [7] are related in the same way as Stepanov’s method and Bombieri’s version of Stepanov’s method are related: 1. Their proof works in a more general setting of an arbitrary algebraic curve, and directly works with Riemann-Roch spaces of algebraic functions on the curve, while our proof works concretely with the equation of the Hermitian curve (and closely related curves), and represents algebraic functions on the curve more explicitly as polynomials. 2.
